processing: A round-rolled, non-oxidised green tea, finished by a slow, low-temperature re-firing in an inclined wok that gives it its shape.
harvest_season: Little is documented about exact dates; spring picking is usual for the class.
appearance_dry: Small, nearly round grains described as seemingly round but not round, with a pale sheen.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear yellow-green, as with other round-rolled Zhejiang greens.
appearance_wet: Green leaves unfurling slowly from the rolled grain.
taste_profile: Little is recorded in detail; as with round-rolled greens generally, expect a firmer, more toasty-green cup than a tender flat tea.

brewing.notes: Typical for rolled pearl-type greens: slightly hotter water and more time than for bud teas, so the grains can open.

vintage_note: Treat it like other Zhejiang greens: current-year spring tea, drunk within the year. It is rare outside its home area, so ask directly for the harvest year. Not to be confused with the far larger trade in Pingshui gunpowder from the same region.
description:
Quangang Huibai is a rolled green tea from Shengzhou in Zhejiang, centred on Quangang village in Xiawang township and Shangwushan village in Guimen township. It is one of the few surviving Chinese round-rolled greens with a name of its own.

What matters is the finish: a slow, low-temperature firing in a tilted wok. It leaves a grain described as seemingly round but not quite round, with the pale sheen the word huibai, shining white, points to.

Cups of this tea are rarely written about in detail. As with similar rolled greens, expect the leaf to need a little more heat and time, and expect some toasty firmness rather than the sweetness of a bud tea.

You will see several spellings, including Qiangang and Shengzhou Hui Bai. It shares a home with Pingshui gunpowder, so check that a pack is what it claims to be.
history: The tea is listed as a Chinese historic famous tea, and one reference says it won fame as a Qing-dynasty court tribute, though the detail behind that claim is thin. Chinese lists of origin teas name it under Shengzhou, then Sheng county, in the form Qiangang Huibai. Little else is documented about who developed it or when.
